title: Bugs that pass a quick read: reviewing AI-generated TypeScript and SQL
description: Find the bugs in AI-written TypeScript, React, browser, Node.js, and SQL code that looks fine at first glance. You'll run into race conditions, security holes, made-up APIs, and assumptions the runtime doesn't share.

questions.title: Why can this search box show results for the wrong query?

options.text: The slower `cat` response can arrive later and overwrite the `caterpillar` results
`encodeURIComponent()` caches the earlier query until the Effect runs again
React always commits Effects in alphabetical order by dependency value
`response.json()` reads from whichever request most recently called `fetch()`

questions.explanation: Each Effect run starts its own request, and responses can come back in any order. If the `cat` request is slower, it calls `setResults` last and wins. Use the Effect's cleanup to ignore the old result, and add an `AbortController` if you also want to cancel the old fetch. React's docs show this exact pattern.
questions.references:
[React: Fetching data with Effects and avoiding race conditions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect#fetching-data-with-effects)

[MDN: `AbortController.abort()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort)

questions.title: What happens to the other two calls when `chargeCard()` rejects first?
questions.description:
```ts
await Promise.all([
  chargeCard(),
  reserveInventory(),
  sendConfirmationEmail(),
]);
```

Assume all three functions start work immediately and share no cancellation signal.

options.text: `Promise.all()` rejects, but the inventory and email operations can keep running
`Promise.all()` rolls back every fulfilled side effect before rejecting
The remaining Promises are automatically aborted at their next `await`
The rejection is delayed until all three operations settle

questions.explanation: `Promise.all()` rejects as soon as any input rejects. That changes only the combined Promise: work that already started keeps going, and nothing gets undone. If you need cancellation, build it into the functions, usually by passing an `AbortSignal`. If you need rollback, write compensating steps or use a transaction.

questions.title: Why is this existence check unsafe when both calls are awaited?

options.text: Another process can change the path between the check and the write
`access()` resolves before the operating system checks the path
`await` permits the two filesystem operations to execute in reverse order
`writeFile()` always follows an internal symlink created by `access()`

questions.explanation: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race. `await` puts your own calls in order, but another process can still change the file in between. The Node docs recommend skipping the check: use the file directly and handle the error. To create a file only if it doesn't exist yet, the `wx` flag checks and creates in one operation, as far as the filesystem guarantees it.

questions.title: Why can `All saved` print before any save finishes?

options.text: `forEach()` does not await its callbacks and returns `undefined`, which `await` accepts immediately
An `async` callback becomes synchronous when passed to an array method
`await` only waits for Promises created directly by `fetch()`
`save()` is automatically moved to a worker thread by `forEach()`

questions.explanation: `forEach()` ignores whatever its callback returns, including the Promises from `async` callbacks. It returns `undefined`, so `await` has nothing to wait for. Use `await Promise.all(records.map(save))` to save everything at once, or a `for...of` loop with `await` to save one at a time.

questions.title: How does this cleanup flag drop a stale response but keep the current one?

options.text: Each Effect run gets its own `ignore` variable, and cleanup flips only that run's copy
React rewrites `ignore` into a component-wide mutex
Cleanup removes the `.then()` callback from the Promise
Setting `ignore` aborts the underlying HTTP request through browser syntax

questions.explanation: Every time the Effect runs, it creates a new `ignore` variable that only that run's `.then()` callback and cleanup can see. When `person` changes, React calls the old cleanup, so only the old callback sees `true`. The new run starts with its own `false`. This skips the stale state update, but the request still runs. Add an `AbortController` if you want to cancel it too.

questions.title: Which changes prevent a lost update in this balance workflow?
questions.description: Two PostgreSQL transactions at the default `READ COMMITTED` level both read a balance of `100`, compute `100 - 10` in application code, and then each run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 90`. Select every approach that works in this simplified case.

options.text: Use one statement such as `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = $1`
Lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before computing and updating it in the transaction
Use `SERIALIZABLE` transactions and retry transactions rejected with a serialization failure
Keep the same read and write statements but add a short sleep before `COMMIT`
Wrap the unchanged workflow in `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`; default isolation alone prevents stale reads

questions.explanation: Under `READ COMMITTED`, wrapping a read-modify-write in a transaction doesn't make it atomic, because both transactions can read the same old value. A relative `UPDATE` lets PostgreSQL subtract from the row's current value at write time. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the row, so the second transaction waits its turn. `SERIALIZABLE` detects the conflict and fails one transaction, and your code has to retry it.

questions.title: What's the safest fix if the name only needs to show up as text?

options.text: Assign the complete message to `greeting.textContent`
Wrap `name` in `<span>` before assigning it to `innerHTML`
Call `encodeURIComponent(name)` and keep using `innerHTML`
Base64-encode `name` and decode it inside the template literal

questions.explanation: `innerHTML` parses its string as HTML, so anyone who controls the URL can inject markup and scripts. `textContent` inserts plain text, which is all this greeting needs. URL encoding and Base64 change how data travels; they don't make HTML safe. If you really need to render user-supplied HTML, use a well-reviewed sanitizer or a Trusted Types policy.

questions.title: Which security checks does this cross-window token handoff need?

options.text: Send with the receiver's exact origin instead of `*`
Verify `event.origin` and, where appropriate, `event.source` before trusting the message
Validate the message's expected shape before using its data
Base64-encode the token so an unintended receiver cannot understand it
Set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the popup; that authenticates `message` events

questions.explanation: An exact `targetOrigin` keeps the token from reaching the popup after it navigates to another site. The receiver has to check who sent the message with `event.origin` (and sometimes `event.source`), then check the data's shape. Base64 hides nothing. CORS controls which sites can read network responses and plays no part in trusting `postMessage` events.

questions.title: What's still missing after this CORS setup?
questions.description:
An API returns private invoices and sets:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example
```

Its handler returns any invoice named by `?invoiceId=...` without checking who is asking or whether they own it.

options.text: Server-side authentication and object-level authorization for each invoice
A longer CORS preflight cache duration
A wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` so every legitimate client works
A JavaScript check that the page's hostname ends with `example`

questions.explanation: CORS tells browsers which origins may read a response from JavaScript. It doesn't check who the caller is or whether they own the invoice, and non-browser clients ignore it entirely. The API has to authenticate the caller and confirm they may see that invoice. Otherwise anyone can change the ID and read someone else's invoice, a bug known as an insecure direct object reference (IDOR).
questions.references:
[OWASP: REST Security Cheat Sheet, CORS](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/REST_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html#cors)

[OWASP: Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.title: Why doesn't `SameSite=Lax` protect this transfer endpoint?
questions.description: The session cookie uses `SameSite=Lax`. The app moves money on `GET /transfer?to=attacker&amount=500`, and the victim clicks an attacker's link to that URL.

options.text: Lax can send cookies on top-level cross-site navigation using a safe HTTP method, so a state-changing GET remains dangerous
Lax sends cookies only when JavaScript calls `fetch()` with a JSON body
GET requests cannot carry cookies under the HTTP specification
SameSite affects only third-party images and never navigation

questions.explanation: `SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies when a user follows a link from another site, as long as the request uses a safe method like GET. If a GET request can move money, a link anywhere can trigger a transfer with the victim's session. Use POST or another non-safe method for changes and add proper CSRF protection. OWASP recommends SameSite only as an extra layer on top of that.

questions.title: Why can't this parameterized query choose the table?

options.text: PostgreSQL parameters represent data values, not identifiers such as table names
PostgreSQL parameters work only in `INSERT` statements
The placeholders must be numbered from `$0`
Both values become safe identifiers if they are converted to uppercase

questions.explanation: Parameters carry data values like `id`. PostgreSQL won't put them where a name belongs, such as a database, schema, table, or column. The safest option is a fixed set of queries chosen through an allowlist. If you truly need a dynamic name, escape it with your driver's identifier-escaping function, and never paste untrusted text into the SQL string.

questions.title: What's wrong with this password-reset token generator?

options.text: `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and must not generate security tokens
Base 36 strings cannot be sent in an HTTP header
`slice(2)` reveals the user's browser language
The token is secure only when `Math.floor()` is applied first

questions.explanation: `Math.random()` is meant for non-security uses and doesn't guarantee unpredictable output. Reset tokens need enough bytes from a cryptographically secure generator, such as Web Crypto's `getRandomValues()` or your server's crypto API. How you encode those bytes afterward is a separate step and doesn't make them more or less secure.

questions.title: Which standard Fetch API call parses this response body?

options.text: Replace `response.parseJSON()` with `response.json()`
Replace it with `response.body.toObject()`
Replace it with `fetch.parse(response)`
Remove `await`; `response.parseJSON()` is synchronous

questions.explanation: `Response` has a `json()` method. It reads the whole body and returns a Promise of the parsed value. `parseJSON()` doesn't exist. Also, a body that parses fine can still come from a failed request, so real code usually checks `response.ok` first.

questions.title: Where does the standard `throwIfAborted()` method live?

options.text: On the signal: `controller.signal.throwIfAborted()`
On the constructor: `AbortController.throwIfAborted(controller)`
On every Promise: `promise.throwIfAborted()`
On `DOMException`: `DOMException.throwIfAborted(controller)`

questions.explanation: The controller does one thing: `abort()`. Everything else lives on its `signal`, including the abort state, the reason, the `abort` event, and `throwIfAborted()`. `signal.throwIfAborted()` throws the abort reason if the signal is already aborted and does nothing otherwise.

questions.title: Which modern JavaScript call groups the orders by status?
questions.description:
The generated code uses the shape of an old proposal:

```ts
const byStatus = orders.groupBy((order) => order.status);
```

options.text: `Object.groupBy(orders, (order) => order.status)`
`Array.groupBy(orders, (order) => order.status)`
`orders.groupByKey("status")`
`Object.prototype.groupBy.call(orders, "status")`

questions.explanation: The standard API is the static `Object.groupBy(items, callback)`. Browsers once tried an array method, but it caused web-compatibility problems, so the design moved to a static method. It returns a null-prototype object whose values are arrays. Use `Map.groupBy()` when the keys shouldn't be converted to property keys.

questions.title: Which built-in replaces this made-up deferred Promise API?
questions.description:
```ts
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.defer();
```

Assume a runtime that supports Baseline 2024 JavaScript features.

options.text: `Promise.withResolvers()`
`Promise.expose()`
`Promise.handlers()`
`Promise.pending()`

questions.explanation: `Promise.withResolvers()` returns a plain object with `promise`, `resolve`, and `reject`. `Promise.defer()` sounds right because some libraries offer a deferred helper, but it isn't standard. `withResolvers()` became Baseline in 2024, so older targets need a fallback or polyfill.

questions.title: Which standard call combines these Sets without changing `permissions`?

options.text: `permissions.union(extra)`
`permissions.concat(extra)`
`Set.merge(permissions, extra)`
`permissions.addAll(extra)`

questions.explanation: `Set.prototype.union()` returns a new Set with every value from both Sets and leaves the original alone. `merge()` doesn't exist. `union()` is fairly new, so for older engines you can build a new Set from both, as in `new Set([...permissions, ...extra])`.

questions.title: What should replace the made-up `localStorage.getJSON()` call?

options.text: Read with `getItem()`, handle `null`, and parse the stored string with `JSON.parse()`
Call `localStorage.parse("preferences")`
Read `localStorage.preferences.json` because Storage values expose format properties
Call `JSON.getItem(localStorage, "preferences")`

questions.explanation: Web Storage stores only strings. `getItem(key)` returns a string or `null`, so storing objects means calling `JSON.stringify()` when you write and `JSON.parse()` when you read. Be ready for a missing key and for stored JSON that's broken or in an old format.

questions.title: What does this function do when the server returns a 404?

options.text: `fetch()` resolves with a `Response`, so the code tries to parse the 404 body instead of jumping to `catch`
`fetch()` rejects with an `HTTPError` before a `Response` exists
`fetch()` retries the request once, then returns `{ kind: "offline" }`
`response.json()` converts every 404 body to `null`

questions.explanation: `fetch()` rejects only when the request itself fails, for example on a network error or a malformed URL. An HTTP error status like 404 still resolves with a `Response`, so check `response.ok` or `response.status` yourself. `response.json()` can also reject on its own if the body isn't valid JSON.

questions.title: What does this code log after the default sort?

options.text: A `TypeError`, because numbers require an explicit comparator

questions.explanation: `sort()` sorts the array in place and returns the same array. Without a comparator, it compares elements as strings, so `"10"` comes before `"2"`. To sort numbers, pass `(a, b) => a - b`. If you want a sorted copy and an untouched original, use `toSorted()` where it's supported.

questions.title: What happens when this payload is serialized without a replacer?

options.text: `JSON.stringify()` throws a `TypeError` because BigInt has no default JSON serialization
It emits `{"invoiceId":9007199254740993}` with exact integer precision
It emits `{"invoiceId":null}`
It silently omits only the trailing `n` and stores an IEEE-754 number

questions.explanation: JSON has no BigInt type, so `JSON.stringify()` throws unless you tell it how to serialize one. Converting a large BigInt to `Number` can lose precision. A common fix is to send it as a decimal string and convert it back on the other side.
questions.references: [MDN: BigInt cannot be serialized in JSON by default](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Errors/BigInt_not_serializable)

questions.title: Does the optional chain prevent an exception here?

options.text: No; `user?.profile` becomes `undefined`, then `.name` throws because the parentheses end the optional chain
Yes; any `?.` anywhere in an expression makes every later property access optional
No; optional chaining cannot be used with `const` values
Yes; the complete expression evaluates to `null`

questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits only within one unbroken chain. The parentheses end the chain, so `user?.profile` gives `undefined`, and the plain `.name` after it throws a `TypeError`. Write `user?.profile?.name` instead, which returns `undefined` here.

questions.title: Starting from zero, what does the count show after one click?

options.text: `1`, because all three calls set the count to the same render's value plus one
`3`, because every setter synchronously mutates `count` before the next line
`0`, because React ignores repeated setters in one handler
The result is nondeterministically `1`, `2`, or `3` depending on CPU scheduling

questions.explanation: `count` is a snapshot from the current render, and calling the setter doesn't change it. All three calls ask for the same value, `1`. To add three, pass an updater function instead: call `setCount((n) => n + 1)` three times, and React gives each call the result of the one before.

questions.title: How private is this TypeScript `private` field at runtime?

options.text: Not private at runtime; TypeScript erases the modifier, and bracket access reads the ordinary property
The JavaScript engine throws a `PrivateFieldError` for bracket access
The field is encrypted in the emitted JavaScript bundle
The field is omitted from emitted JavaScript and always reads as `undefined`

questions.explanation: TypeScript checks `private` only at compile time and removes it from the emitted JavaScript, so it isn't a security boundary. JavaScript's own `#code` private fields are enforced at runtime. Neither one can hide a real secret in client code, because the user controls that code and where it runs.
